<reason>Side B won the decisive clashes. Its pressure questions extracted two real concessions from PRO: that Australia's boats stopped outright (granting at least one enforcement regime collapsed irregular migration with no visa scheme) and that seasonal permits "wouldn't" stop Honduran families or Syrians—the populations that dominate actual irregular flows. B then leveraged both concessions into a coherent weighing story ("a lever that cannot move the largest weight"). B also flipped PRO's strongest overstay attack with the memorable "you cannot call overstays the unfixable leak and then propose to multiply the pipes," and its "spending, not deterrence" reframing cleanly answered PRO's question about four decades of US budgets. B's Bracero rebuttal—crediting the 1954 drop to the enforcement campaign rather than the visa—was sharper and more historically plausible than PRO's counterclaim. PRO fought well: the rerouting critique of EU-Turkey and Israel, the "scarcity concedes missing legal supply" point, and the closing flip that overstay tools police a visa system were all genuinely strong. But B's closing inverted that flip effectively (exit tracking and interior removal are enforcement), and PRO's residual case—single working-age labor migrants under binding caps—was left defending a narrowing share of the flow. Both sides were grounded and civil; B simply made the debate easier to decide and controlled the endgame.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.1-B4.2: CON's answer to the overstay pressure—"Every seasonal visa is a future overstay decision... You cannot call overstays the unfixable leak and then propose to multiply the pipes," plus the point that overstays became a majority only because border enforcement crushed the other source ("enforcement's success reweighting the denominator"). This single exchange neutralized PRO's best pressure question and turned it into CON's own weapon for the rest of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
